analysis.one_liner: Bars doctors and hospitals from sending patients surprise bills for out-of-network emergency and hospital care.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 110 cosponsors from both parties but was referred to four committees and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When someone goes to an emergency room or an in-network hospital, they can be treated by a doctor who is not in their insurance network and then billed for the difference on top of what they already owe. This bill would make those visits count as in-network for the patient, require insurers to pay providers a negotiated or arbitrator-set rate, penalize providers that bill patients beyond their normal cost-sharing, and add tools like deductibles printed on insurance cards, provider directories, and a one-year limit on billing patients after care.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured patients who get emergency care or scheduled care at in-network hospitals would no longer be stuck with large out-of-network bills they had no way to avoid. The protections would also cover federal employees' plans, and states with their own balance-billing laws could keep them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured patients facing surprise medical bills

how_it_helps.text: Patients would owe no more out of pocket for out-of-network emergency care than they would for in-network care, and those payments would count toward their deductible and out-of-pocket maximum.

Care at an in-network hospital, lab, or imaging center would be billed at in-network cost-sharing even when the individual doctor involved was out of network, including imaging and lab services ordered by an in-network provider.
Insurers and providers would settle payment through negotiation first, then a binding independent arbitration process, with the losing side paying the arbitrator's fees.
Providers that bill patients more than the allowed cost-sharing would face civil money penalties unless they refund the patient within 30 days.

Insurance cards would have to show in-network and out-of-network deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums, insurers would have to maintain audited provider directories, and providers could not bill a patient for a service more than a year after the date of service.

analysis.who_pays: Out-of-network emergency physicians, anesthesiologists, radiologists, and other specialists would lose the ability to bill patients directly for the balance, leaving them to negotiate with insurers. Health insurers and employers that fund plans would pay the disputed amounts instead of patients, and premiums could rise if arbitration pushes payments up.

drawbacks.text: The arbitration process tells arbitrators to consider the 80th percentile of charges in the area as a reference point, a benchmark that tends to favor providers and could push up out-of-network payment rates and, over time, premiums.

The bill does not set a fixed payment rate; insurers initially pay a rate they determine to be commercially reasonable, which could invite disputes and administrative costs that get passed into premiums.
Federal rules would not apply in states that have their own balance-billing laws, so protections would vary by state for most plans.
Penalties for improper billing are enforced by the Secretary of Health and Human Services at amounts the Secretary determines, which makes the strength of the enforcement uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is strong: a patient cannot be billed extra for care they could not shop for, and penalties back that up. The main honest cost is that moving the money fight from patients to insurers and providers adds an arbitration system whose cost and effect on premiums depends heavily on how the rules are written, and the 80th-percentile reference point leans toward providers. On balance the bill transfers a real burden off patients, at a modest and uncertain cost spread across premiums.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees and then to a Health subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended, never reaching a floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 26, 2019 by Rep. Raul Ruiz and referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Reform, and Education and Labor Committees.
The next day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress.
It had 110 cosponsors, including 61 of the 197 House Republicans and 49 of the 231 House Democrats, but no committee ever reported it and the House never voted on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Out-of-network providers kept their ability to bill patients the balance on emergency and hospital care, and insurers and providers kept the existing arrangement rather than a new arbitration system. The one-fourth of House members who backed the bill got nothing for their support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Providers who balance-bill patients kept that power

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was split across both parties: 61 of the 197 House Republicans and 49 of the 231 House Democrats signed on, and the bill died in committee anyway.

industries.industry: Out-of-network physicians and specialists (emergency medicine, anesthesiology, radiology)
industries.note: These providers currently bill patients directly for the amount insurers do not cover when patients cannot choose them. The bill ends that revenue channel and forces payment through negotiation or arbitration instead.

Hospitals and emergency departments could no longer hold patients liable above the allowed cost-sharing and would face civil penalties if they did, though they could recover the balance from insurers instead.

Insurers gain leverage because they set the initial commercially reasonable rate for out-of-network care, but they take on the disputed payment amounts that previously fell on patients, plus new reporting, directory, and card-disclosure duties.
